citations.context: argues under Pennsylvania law that fraud claims based on pre-contractual misrepresentations that induced the contract can survive an integration clause, and references the gist of the action doctrine or cites Pennsylvania authority

first_check.explanation: The gist-of-the-action doctrine is real Pennsylvania law. eToll, 811 A.2d 10 (Pa. Super. 2002), suggests fraud in the inducement is often collateral to the contract and so may escape the doctrine. But the rubric's main proposition is that fraud claims based on pre-contract statements that induced the contract survive an integration clause, and that is wrong. Toy v. Metropolitan Life, 928 A.2d 186 (Pa. 2007), one of the cases the rubric names, together with Yocca, holds the reverse. Under the parol evidence rule, a fully integrated agreement supersedes earlier representations when fraud in the inducement is alleged. Only fraud in the execution (a term fraudulently left out of the writing) is excepted. The gist-of-the-action point is supportable; the integration-clause point contradicts controlling Pennsylvania Supreme Court authority.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Toy: "this Court has determined that in Pennsylvania, only fraud in the execution ... is excepted from the parol evidence rule's operation"; "when fraud in the execution is alleged, representations made prior to contract formation are not considered superseded and disclaimed by a fully integrated written agreement, as they are when fraud in the inducement is asserted." eToll: "fraud in the inducement of a contract would not necessarily be covered by doctrine because fraud to induce a person to enter into a contract is generally collateral to ... the terms of the contract itself."

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. I read Toy v. Metropolitan Life, 928 A.2d 186 (Pa. 2007), on CourtListener. Restating Yocca, Toy says that "while parol evidence may be introduced based on a party's claim that there was fraud in the execution of a contract, i.e., that a term was fraudulently omitted from the contract, parol evidence may not be admitted based on a claim that there was fraud in the inducement of the contract, i.e., that an opposing party made false representations that induced the complaining party to agree to the contract." It also says that in Pennsylvania "only fraud in the execution ... is excepted from the parol evidence rule's operation." Toy's claim survived only because it was fraud in the execution, so prior representations were "not considered superseded and disclaimed by a fully integrated written agreement, as they are when fraud in the inducement is asserted." The rubric cites Toy for the claim that fraud claims based on pre-contract misrepresentations that induced the contract can survive an integration clause. That is the reverse of Toy's statement of the rule. The MSA here has a fully integrated entire-agreement clause with a non-reliance clause (§ 14.1). A narrow argument remains that representations outside the contract's subject matter escape the rule, but Toy does not stand for the general proposition. eToll's gist-of-the-action point is a separate doctrine and does not cure the integration-clause misstatement.

citations.authority: Temporal proximity as evidence of retaliatory causation (Title VII)
citations.cited_for: Close temporal proximity alone suffices to support an inference of causation
quotes: This close temporal proximity is, standing alone, sufficient to support an inference of causation.
citations.context: Plaintiff's actual termination followed on March 17, 2023, only thirty-five (35) days after the protected activity. This close temporal proximity is, standing alone, sufficient to support an inference of causation.

first_check.quote_check: The quoted sentence is the plaintiff's own assertion and is not attributed to any authority, so there is nothing to match.
first_check.explanation: No authority is cited. The categorical rule stated, that close timing alone suffices, overstates controlling law. This case is in the N.D. Ill., where Seventh Circuit law governs. That court holds that suspicious timing alone rarely suffices and usually needs other supporting evidence. Only in 'egregious cases' does timing alone create a triable issue. Breeden (U.S. 2001) accepts timing alone only where it is 'very close.' The 12-day gap to the termination recommendation might qualify as egregious, but the blanket statement that timing 'standing alone' is sufficient contradicts the general rule.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Milligan v. Bd. of Trs. of S. Ill. Univ., 686 F.3d 378 (7th Cir. 2012): "In egregious cases, suspicious timing alone might create a triable issue on causation" ... "[c]lose temporal proximity provides evidence of causation and may permit a plaintiff to survive summary judgment provided that there is other evidence that supports the inference of a causal link."; Breeden: temporal proximity "must be 'very close'"

second_check.explanation: The finding holds and the evidence for it is stronger than the first check showed. The case is in the N.D. Ill., so Seventh Circuit law governs. Sweet v. Town of Bargersville, 18 F.4th 273 (7th Cir. 2021), quotes Kidwell v. Eisenhauer, 679 F.3d 957, 966 (7th Cir. 2012): "suspicious timing will rarely be sufficient in and of itself to create a triable issue." It also says "we typically allow no more than a few days to elapse between the protected activity and the adverse action," and adds: "In Kidwell we held that a two-month gap and a five-week gap were not close enough to establish probative suspicious timing." The 35-day gap to termination here is the same five-week gap Kidwell rejected. The response's flat statement that this proximity is "standing alone, sufficient to support an inference of causation" misstates the governing rule. The 12-day gap to the termination recommendation is a stronger fact, but the response's categorical sentence covers both gaps. No authority is cited; the defect is in the legal proposition itself.
